sections.b: Jeremiah stood in the gate of the Temple and told the worshipers that the chant "the LORD's temple, the LORD's temple, the LORD's temple" was a lie. The people believed Zion could not fall, as it had not fallen to Sennacherib in 701 BC. Jeremiah said the building protects no one who steals, murders, swears falsely and worships Baal, and then comes to the house "called by my name" and says "We are rescued." He pointed to Shiloh, the earlier sanctuary that God had let be destroyed, and warned that Jerusalem would go the same way. Chapter 26 tells that the priests and prophets wanted him killed for it, and the elders saved him by recalling Micah. Jesus used the sermon's phrase "a cave for bandits" when he drove the traders from the Temple.
sections.refs: Jeremiah 7:1–15; Jeremiah 26:1–19; Matthew 21:13; Mark 11:17; Luke 19:46; Psalm 46:4–5

sections.b: Jeremiah tells the people to "go to my place that was in Shiloh, where I first made my name live" and see what the LORD did to it (7:12, 14; 26:6, 9). Shiloh had held the tent and the ark in the days of Eli and Samuel (1 Samuel 1–4; Psalm 78:60). It was already a ruin in Jeremiah's day. Excavations found a destroyed city from about 1050 BC. The argument is that God's house is not a charm: if he let his own sanctuary fall for his people's sins, he can let Jerusalem fall.

Jeremiah 7:31 names the high places of Topheth in the valley of Ben-hinnom, where people burned their sons and daughters in the fire. The LORD says he never commanded it and it never came up in his heart. Josiah had defiled the place (2 Kings 23:10), but the practice is still accused in Jeremiah's day. The prophet renames the valley the Valley of Slaughter (7:32; 19:6). The word Molech does not appear in chapter 7; Jeremiah 32:35 ties the valley to Molech. For the debate about whether the children were killed, see the sections on Molech elsewhere on this page.

sections.h: The Valley of Ben-hinnom before Gehenna
sections.b: The English word hell in some Bibles stands for Gehenna, the Greek form of Ge Hinnom, the valley south of Jerusalem. Jeremiah is where the valley gets its dark name: people burned children there (7:31), and the LORD says he will make it a Valley of Slaughter where the dead are buried for lack of room and left to the birds (7:32–33). Jeremiah says nothing about the afterlife. The idea that the valley was Jerusalem's burning garbage dump is first reported in the commentary of Radak (about AD 1200) and has no support in sources from Jesus' day (Bailey).

sections.h: The ban on prayer in Jeremiah (7:16; 11:14)
sections.b: Prophets are expected to plead for the people. In Jeremiah the LORD forbids it three times in the early chapters: "do not pray on behalf of this people" (7:16; 11:14; 14:11), and says even Moses and Samuel could not turn him back (15:1). The ban does not mean prayer is wrong. It means the verdict has been given and that the prophet's usual task has changed. The same book keeps Jeremiah's later pleas (14:7–9, 19–22). In 2 Maccabees 15:14 Jeremiah is shown still praying for the people after his death, which Catholic and Orthodox Christians cite for the intercession of the saints.

Jeremiah 7:22 says the LORD did not speak to the ancestors or command them about burnt offering and sacrifice on the day he brought them out of Egypt, only to listen to his voice. The verse is read as a Hebrew idiom of priority (obedience before offerings), as a statement about the day of the exodus before the Sinai laws, as an argument that the Ten Commandments contain no sacrifice (Radak), or as evidence on the age of the sacrifice laws. The same priority is in Hosea 6:6, 1 Samuel 15:22 and Psalm 51:16–17.

In Jeremiah 11 the LORD sends the prophet to proclaim "the words of this covenant" in the cities of Judah. The covenant goes back to the day of the exodus, "the iron furnace," with the formula "you will be my people and I will be your God" (11:4; also 7:23). A curse falls on anyone who does not listen (11:3), Jeremiah answers "Amen," and the LORD says Judah and Israel have broken the covenant by returning to their ancestors' idolatry (11:10). Whether this is Sinai or Josiah's covenant of 622 BC (2 Kings 23:1–3) is debated.

sections.h: Shuv: turning away and turning back
sections.b: Jeremiah's word for repentance is shuv, "turn." The same word means turning away from God (apostasy) and turning back (return). In 8:4–6 the pun is the whole poem: Judah "turned away with a turning that never ends" and "refuses to turn back." In 12:15 the verb is used of God: he too will "turn again" and show compassion on the nations he uprooted. Jeremiah 18:7–10 says the LORD may change course if a nation turns.

Jeremiah charges the prophets and priests with healing the nation's wound "as though it were nothing" and crying "Peace, peace" when there was no peace. The same lines are in 6:13–15, and the Greek lacks them here. The test Jeremiah applies is not the prophets' claim to inspiration but whether they call people to turn. Jeremiah 23:9–40 and chapters 27–28 apply the test to named prophets.

The prophet's lament is mixed with God's. In 8:18–9:3 Jeremiah mourns for the "breaking of my dear people," asks "Is there no balm in Gilead?" and wishes his head were water and his eyes a fountain of tears. In 9:17–22 the LORD himself calls for the women who wail. In 10:19–25 a speaker, perhaps Zion, grieves her torn tent and prays to be corrected with justice. In 12:7–13 the LORD laments his abandoned house. Jewish tradition makes Jeremiah the weeping prophet and the author of Lamentations.

Jeremiah's first confession ends with a complaint: "Why does the way of the wicked go well?" It is the question of Job 21 and Psalm 73. God does not explain. He asks the prophet if he can last when the race gets harder, and tells him that even his own family has turned against him. Before this, Jeremiah says he was "like a tame lamb led away to slaughter" when the men of Anathoth plotted to kill him (11:19), words Christians have read beside Isaiah 53:7.

sections.h: The question of the prosperous wicked
sections.b: Deuteronomy promised blessing for obedience and curse for disobedience. Jeremiah asks, "Why does the way of the wicked go well?" (12:1), as Job and Psalm 73 do. His own experience, plotted against and betrayed by his family, runs against the promise too. The book answers not with a theory but by pointing to the coming judgment (12:3) and to the LORD's own grief (12:7–13).

Jeremiah 10 mocks idols as a tree cut from the forest, shaped by a craftsman, decorated with silver and gold, fastened with nails and hammers, and carried because it cannot walk. It is "a scarecrow in a cucumber patch" that can do neither harm nor good. The LORD, by contrast, made the earth by his power and the sky by his understanding. The mockery is like Isaiah 40:18–20 and 44:9–20 and Psalm 115. The Letter of Jeremiah (Baruch 6) expands it. Verse 11, the only Aramaic sentence in the book, says the gods who did not make the heavens and the earth will perish.

uncommon: Some scholars think the satire in Isaiah 40–48 and Jeremiah 10 is later than Jeremiah; others date it to his time.

sections.b: Jeremiah charges Judah with sending up smoke to Baal (7:9; 11:13, 17), following "the Baals" their ancestors taught them (9:14) and teaching the neighbors' oath formulas (12:16). The altars to "the Shame" (bosheth), a scribe's word for Baal, were as many as the streets of Jerusalem (11:13). In 12:16 the LORD says that if the neighbors who taught his people to swear by Baal now learn to swear by him, they will be built up among his people.

sections.h: Circumcised in body, uncircumcised in heart (Jeremiah 9:25–26)
sections.b: The LORD says he will punish "everyone circumcised in a foreskin" (a riddle in the Hebrew): Egypt, Judah, Edom, Ammon, Moab and the desert tribes. All the nations are uncircumcised, and all Israel is uncircumcised in heart. Deuteronomy 10:16 and 30:6 had already spoken of circumcising the heart; Jeremiah 4:4 does too. Paul takes up the idea (Romans 2:25–29), and Colossians 2:11 speaks of a circumcision not made by hands.
sections.refs: Jeremiah 9:25–26; Jeremiah 4:4; Deuteronomy 10:16; Deuteronomy 30:6; Romans 2:25–29; Colossians 2:11

sections.h: Wormwood and poisoned water in Jeremiah
sections.b: Jeremiah 9:15 says the LORD will feed the people wormwood and give them poisoned water to drink, and 8:14 says the people themselves know they have been made to drink poisoned water. The image is the bitter fruit of a root that turns from the LORD (Deuteronomy 29:18) and returns in 23:15 and Lamentations 3:15, 19.

sections.h: Boast in loyal love, justice and righteousness (Jeremiah 9:23–24)
sections.b: Jeremiah 9:24 says the one who boasts should boast in knowing the LORD, who acts in loyal love (hesed), justice and righteousness on the earth, "for in these things I delight." Knowing God means sharing his ways: Jeremiah says Josiah knew him by defending the poor (22:15–16). Paul's "let the one who boasts boast in the Lord" (1 Corinthians 1:31) condenses the passage.

sections.h: The wise and the scribes in Jeremiah 8–9
sections.b: Jeremiah says the people claim "We are wise, and the LORD's law is with us," but the scribes' lying pen has turned the law into a lie (8:8). The wise will be shamed because they have thrown out the LORD's word (8:9). Chapter 9 adds that the wise, strong and rich should not boast, but should boast that they know the LORD (9:23–24). Compare the wise who counsel in 18:18.

In Jeremiah 8:3 the survivors of the evil family, scattered by the LORD to many lands, will choose death over life. The remnant, usually a sign of hope in the prophets, is here a sign of a wretched survival (compare 11:23, where Anathoth is to have no remnant at all, and 12:15, where a restored remnant is promised).

Jeremiah 12:14–17 turns the verbs of his call, "uproot," on the neighbors who touched Judah's land, and then offers them a return: after the uprooting the LORD will have compassion, and if they learn to swear by his name they will be "built up among my people." If they refuse, the uprooting is final. The collection of oracles against the nations is in 46–51.

Jeremiah 10:21 says the shepherds have acted stupidly and have not looked for the LORD, so the flock is scattered. In 12:10 "many shepherds" have wrecked the LORD's vineyard. They may be Judah's leaders or the invading generals. Ezekiel 34 develops the image.

sections.h: The Queen of Heaven in Jeremiah 7
sections.b: Jeremiah 7:18 shows whole households working together: children gather wood, fathers light the fire, women knead dough for cakes for the Queen of Heaven, and drink offerings are poured out to other gods. The LORD tells Jeremiah to stop praying for the people (7:16), and describes the worship as an insult that falls on the worshipers' own heads (7:19). The title means a goddess, usually Ishtar or Astarte, though no inscription found in Judah uses the title. Aramaic letters from Hermopolis in Egypt (late sixth or early fifth century BC) greet a temple of the Queen of Heaven at Syene, and the Jewish colony at Elephantine swore by Anat-Yahu, but these are later than Jeremiah and scholars disagree on what they show about Judah. The Greek says "army of heaven." See Jeremiah 44:15–25 for the women's reply, and the chapter 7 card on Christian use of the title for Mary.

sections.h: Jeremiah 7–12: the sermon, the plot and the complaint
sections.b: These chapters hold the Temple sermon (7), the first collections of laments (8:18–9:3; 10:17–25), the idol satire (10:1–16), the covenant sermon (11:1–17), the plot of his own village, Anathoth (11:18–23), and the first of his "confessions," in which he asks why the wicked prosper (12:1–6). For the first time in the book the prophet is shown as someone in danger from his neighbors and relatives and arguing with God.
